paragraphs: The following judgments concern the on-site way of working of locksmiths and safe repairers and do not predict hiring, qualification, authorization, or contract outcomes.

The core of a locksmith and safe repairer is turning lock and safe problems into deliverable safety repairs: opening locks and repairing locks, duplicating and making keys, changing lock cylinders and combinations; installing and repairing safes, vault doors, and components; establishing and maintaining master key systems; and installing door locks, door closers, and other door hardware along with alarm and electronic access control systems, while keeping key and work records.

A completely fictional work sample: present a fictional lock and safe service scenario (including 1 set of lock cylinders and keys to be replaced, 1 master key system change, 1 safe that cannot be opened, and 1 door hardware installation), requiring you to write out an opening/replacement plan, key making and records, and anomaly handling and escalation within 60 minutes; do not use real customers, access control data, or employer secrets.

Sample output and reflection: check whether you first verified customer identity and authorization, whether you chose the plan by the mechanical and electronic structure, and whether you kept key and work records; then ask yourself whether you can stay cautious when facing no-key opening and safe work, whether you can honestly handle other people's property and access control information, and whether you are willing to take responsibility for safety and records.

On this page, locksmiths and safe repairers means O*NET 49-9094.00: repairing and opening locks, duplicating and making keys, changing lock cylinders and safe combinations, and installing and repairing safes and vault doors; opening door locks with lock-picking tools when there is no key, establishing and maintaining master key systems, and installing door locks, door closers, and other door hardware as well as alarm and electronic access control systems. The work is mainly shop and on-site service, emphasizing safety, integrity, and accurate records. This page does not cover adjacent positions such as electricians, plumbers, or elevator installers and repairers.

entries: Objects of work: mechanical and electronic locks, lock cylinders and key blanks, safes and vault doors, master key systems and key records, door locks and door closers and other door hardware, alarm and electronic access control equipment, and customer authorization and work orders.

Checkable outputs: verified opening or replacement records, keys made to bitting or coding, an updated master key system and key ledger, locks and safes installed or repaired to standard, and anomaly and escalation records.

Complete workflow: accept the work order and verify customer identity and authorization → judge the lock/safe structure and the opening plan → open the lock or change the cylinder and make keys → install or repair locks, safes, and door hardware → establish or update the master key system and ledger → test and hand over → record and invoice.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether customer identity and authorization are sufficient, which opening or replacement plan suits the lock and safe structure, which tasks require specialized tools or qualifications, when to stop and recommend replacement rather than opening, and which electronic access control matters must be handed to the authorized party.

Environment and rhythm: mainly shop and on-site service, often standing, using hand tools, and carrying a tool box; you may face drilling, cutting, and welding environments and must also communicate authorization and fees with customers, and the rhythm is driven by work orders and emergency calls.

Research inputs: the occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, interest code, and tool and technology information of O*NET 49-9094.00; the research conclusions are used within the precise U.S. occupation scope and are not used to infer qualifications, wages, or employment framing in mainland China.

What is checked first: customer identity and proof of ownership, work authorization and the work order scope, the structure and model of the lock and safe, the required key blanks and parts, the on-site safety conditions, and the opening and replacement records that must be retained.

Work loop: starting from accepting the work order and verifying authorization, through judging the structure and opening plan, opening or replacing, making keys, installing and repairing, and updating the master key system, to test handover and records; the next step is not taken before any authorization or structural judgment is confirmed.

Adjacent duty boundaries: this page covers only locksmiths and safe repairers; electricians handle electrical systems, plumbers handle water supply and drainage, and elevator installers and repairers handle elevators and escalators, and the authority and final responsibility for building systems outside door hardware and access control must not be swapped with this page.

General maintenance and repair workers handle multiple types of building and equipment faults according to work orders, with a broader scope; locksmiths and safe repairers focus on locks, keys, safes, and door hardware, with more concentrated skills and authorization.

Security and fire alarm systems installers focus on installing and commissioning alarm and detection systems; locksmiths and safe repairers also install electronic access control on top of locks and safes but usually do not take on fire system design and acceptance.

Mechanical door repairers repair the mechanics and drives of automatic doors, rolling doors, and other door bodies; locksmiths and safe repairers handle locks, keys, and safes, and door hardware is only part of it.

Machinery maintenance workers install and calibrate industrial machinery and equipment; locksmiths and safe repairers center on lock, key, and safe safety, with different work objects and authorization.
The AI impact boundary for locksmiths and safe repairers

Editorial trial candidates: use fictional work orders to test model data retrieval and work ledger organization; the existence of key machines, lock databases, or access control systems is not equal to AI capability, adoption, or effect. Customer authorization, structural judgment, and key and access control results must be verified by the responsible person. AI Impact Score 8% is an editorial estimate. Model impact index for three equally weighted representative core tasks; not a measured share of working time or a job-loss probability. floor((25+0+0)/3+0.5)=8; fermatmind-ai-impact-v1; 2026-10-18.The three tasks, ratings and sources are listed in the FermatMind method source record on this page.

The occupational source states the tasks and objects this occupation actually handles (lock opening and repair, key making, safes and vaults, door hardware and access control, key ledgers); tool capability, organizational adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately, and wage or employment data are not used to replace AI evidence.

Editorial task breakdown: the assistive steps above are candidates pending verification. This round obtained no ranking of automation difficulty by step or actual adoption effects, and on-site judgment and authorization responsibility are confirmed by the position's responsible person.

Human control points are verifying customer identity and proof of ownership, judging the lock and safe structure and plan, deciding to stop or replace, and taking responsibility for work records and the key ledger.

First use a completely fictional lock and safe work order for an offline plan exercise, recording the authorization check, the plan, and the escalation path, without relying on unverified databases or prompts to replace on-site judgment.
Editorial suggestion: tools can assist with specification retrieval, key coding, and permission registration; the current material does not prove that this occupation generally adopts these systems.
Customer authorization and on-site structural judgment take precedence, and human verification and work records are retained.

Mainland China wage boundary: this round's industry material did not establish a separately listed wage correspondence for locksmiths and safe repairers. The resident services and repair industry annual average serves only as a related-service enterprise proxy, does not prove that all locksmiths fall in that industry, and does not include self-employed personal income.

Framing note: the National Bureau of Statistics 2025 average annual wages of employed persons in resident services, repair, and other services were {{fact:cn-repair-nonprivate-wage}} for urban non-private units and {{fact:cn-repair-private-wage}} for urban private units; the national urban non-private unit total was {{fact:cn-national-nonprivate-wage}}. These are industry framings and are not equal to this occupation's median or starting pay.

Category boundary: the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security enterprise pay survey information is published by occupation/position classification and can be used to look up pay for related repair and service positions, but this page obtained no entry precisely corresponding to O*NET 49-9094.00 and does not treat it as this occupation's national median; the competent department's publication prevails.

Insufficient evidence: no national occupational wage median, statistical period, or framing corresponding to locksmiths and safe repairers in mainland China was obtained; this page shows only the industry proxy and marks it as an industry framing, without filling the gap with proxy figures or U.S. figures.
U.S. wage and employment framing for locksmiths and safe repairers

The U.S. national 2025 OEWS wage percentiles are in the table below; the median wage and hourly value are used separately according to the original occupation source. The employment projection is separately 18,700 in 2025 and 16,500 in 2035, growth of -12% from 2025 to 2035, with average annual openings of 1,200 (growth and replacements).

The wage percentiles are U.S. OEWS occupational wage statistics, not self-employment business income; this round obtained no general prevalence of hourly/piece-rate pay or on-site overtime pay arrangements, and the contract and fee model are verified position by position.

The 10th and 90th percentiles are the boundaries of this occupation's U.S. national wage distribution and do not correspond to novice or senior levels; the percentile table cannot decompose the effects of education, experience, region, or employer.

O*NET2025 industry employment share: administrative and support services 54%, educational services 11%. Sub-industries that are not shown are not allocated on our own; a share is not a wage or future hiring demand.

2025 employment 18,700, growth of -12% from 2025 to 2035. Average annual openings of 1,200 include replacements and are not current job postings or the number of people added each year; no personal opportunity or AI causality is inferred.
Fit signals: start with observable work behaviors

To judge suitability, first look at whether you can patiently take apart mechanical and electronic structures, whether you can stay cautious in no-key opening and safe work, whether you can honestly handle other people's property and access control information, and whether you are willing to take responsibility for work records and safety; tools such as RIASEC can only raise hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.
Positive signals: strong hands-on ability, liking to study locks and mechanical structures, cautious and meticulous, honest and reliable, and willing to record according to procedure.

Caution conditions: people who lack patience, tend to skip authorization checks under customer pressure, are unwilling to learn electronic and mechanical structure updates, or find it hard to honestly handle other people's property and access control information need to be careful.

Exercise actions: with a completely fictional lock and safe work order, complete one authorization check, plan selection, and work record exercise, and ask someone else to review it against the record.

The RIASEC interest code is RC (Realistic—Conventional): inclined to hands-on repair of mechanical and electronic equipment and to working according to procedure; the related labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualification authorization.

Insufficient evidence: this round obtained no personality predictive validity research for locksmiths and safe repairers. Observe structural understanding, authorization checking, and recording behavior with your own training setup or fictional work orders; personality tools are for reflection only.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and can only be used for self-reflection.

Entry paths and ability stages

The O*NET education survey found 62% of respondents thought new entrants need a high school diploma or equivalent, 15% a post-secondary certificate, and 8% less than high school, which is not the incumbent education distribution. JobZone1—2, from a few days to one year of training, is a group description and not a fixed entry period for locksmiths; actual position and local requirements are verified separately.

United States: California BSIS clearly distinguishes locksmith business licensing from employee registration, which is a state example and is not extrapolated across the whole country. Mainland China: the Jinan public security reply of 2026 mentions information collection and registration for units that have lawfully obtained a business license, which is a local management example. Insufficient evidence: a complete correspondence between national individual qualifications and local business/work requirements has not yet been established, and it cannot be asserted that there is no uniform qualification.

Training certificates, vendor certifications, and work authorization are different states: certification does not automatically grant lock opening, safe work, or access control management authority; matters beyond the position and authorization scope should be handed to personnel with authority.
Entry stage: practice lock disassembly and assembly, key making, and door hardware installation under supervision, learn the authorization and record processes, and keep evidence of the work process.

Showcase evidence: use a reviewable work record, a key making and master key system description, and an explanatory plan for a safe or access control job to show execution according to procedure and accuracy.

Next step: check the registration and practice requirements of the target employer or self-employment location, the tools and training required, and verify lock opening, replacement, and record ability in supervised real work orders.

Editorial target examples: safes, electronic access control, and business or technical management require separately filling in specialized training, applicable licensing registration, and customer authorization; growing seniority does not automatically allow expanding the work scope.
Market signals and transition directions

U.S. O*NET/BLS: 2025 employment 18,700, projected 16,500 in 2035, growth of -12% from 2025 to 2035, average annual openings 1,200 (growth and replacements). An occupational projection is not a current recruitment sample or a personal hiring probability.

O*NET2025 industry employment share: administrative and support services 54%, educational services 11%. Sub-industries that are not shown are not allocated on our own; a share is not a wage or future hiring demand.

Transferable abilities: lock and mechanical disassembly and assembly, key making and master key systems, safe and door hardware installation, customer authorization and record management, and safety and tool use.

Moving to general repair requires filling in target equipment fault diagnosis, maintenance, and mechanical installation evidence and checking specialized work qualifications; the original lock experience does not automatically cover building electrical, plumbing, or elevators.

risks.scenario: When key and work records are incomplete or not updated.

title.text: Locksmith and safe repairer career judgment: work, entry, and risk boundaries

subject.name: Locksmiths and safe repairers
subject.summary: On this page this means O*NET 49-9094.00 locksmiths and safe repairers: opening and repairing locks, duplicating and making keys (including cutting to bitting or by coding machine), changing lock cylinders and safe combinations, and installing and repairing safes, vault doors, and components; opening door locks with lock-picking tools when there is no key, establishing and maintaining master key systems, installing door locks and door closers and other door hardware, and installing alarm and electronic access control systems. The work is mainly shop and on-site service and involves tools such as mechanical and electronic locks, key machines, and drills, emphasizing safety, integrity, and accurate records. This page does not cover adjacent positions such as electricians, plumbers, or elevator installers and repairers.
